newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metal employers meet as new deal signed.
newsitem.headline: German metal employers meet as new deal signed.

text.p: Germany's metal and engineering employers came increasingly under siege on Sunday as it emerged that a new regional wage deal had been signed guaranteeing workers full sick pay.

The Gesamtmetall employers federation had earlier begun a board meeting at which they were expected to attack a wage deal signed on Thursday in the state of Lower Saxony that did not implement a new law allowing cuts to sick payments.

But IG Metall, the powerful trade union which has already led mass protests in the industry to keep sick pay at full wages, said on Sunday a similar deal had now been agreed in part of the big southern state of Baden-Wuerttemberg.

An IG Metall spokesman said negotiators there had agreed overnight on Thursday a package for around 300,000 workers in the south of the region which mirrored the Lower Saxony deal "in all the main points".

The earlier agreement, which applies to some 90,000 workers, also included a wage rise of 1.5 percent in 1997 and 2.5 percent in 1998. Union negotiators had in return agreed to lower holiday and other bonuses.
IG Metall, which in total has close to three million members, has warned that all-out strikes are possible next year if deals are not concluded nationwide protecting full sick pay.

Nobody was immediately available from Gesamtmetall, which was holding a damage-limitation meeting at Frankfurt airport, to confirm that the deal had been reached in the southern part of Baden-Wuerttemberg.
Earlier, Klaus Fritsche, negotiator for the employers federation in north of Baden-Wuerttemberg, had said neither his section nor neighbouring Bavaria could agree such a deal.
Gesamtmetall business manager Thomas Vajna had also said he thought it would be "very surprising" if the Gesamtmetall board would offer any concrete recommendation of the agreement to other regions.
The Welt am Sonntag newspaper had earlier said the meeting would reject the deal struck in Lower Saxony state on Thursday as a pacesetter for pay rounds in metals and engineering.

The cut in sick pay to 80 percent is allowed under austerity laws passed by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government this autumn to boost job creation in Germany, suffering from record post-unification unemployment of four million.

IG Metall has already held protests involving hundreds of thousands of workers to defend the sick pay allowances at full wages. It declared victory on Thursday in Lower Saxony when employers guaranteed full sick pay entitlements into the next century.
IG Metall chief Klaus Zwickel called in Welt am Sonntag for the local pay deal, which covers 90,000 workers, to be agreed "quickly and without a lot of noise" countrywide.
If no deal is reached, then strike action could begin in Bavaria from March 1, when a binding pledge not to down tools expires, he warned.

Gesamtmetall is battling to contain wage costs in an industry which is losing over 100,000 jobs a year, but its hard line on sick pay has been undermined by what Welt am Sonntag called an unprecedented breaking of ranks in Lower Saxony.
